name: A Land Grant in a Splintered Kamarupa
summary: Brahmin recipients receive a village grant inscribed on copper plates from a local king (Udayakarna's inscription is dated 1185), in a Kamarupa that has broken into small domains after the Palas. The scene shows the mechanism that later produced landholding intermediaries and the Baro-Bhuyans.
notes: The 12th-century 'lunar dynasty' is a reconstructed list of names (Bhaskara, Rayarideva, Udayakarna, Vallabhadeva); no narrative survives. Artistic reconstruction; keep temple architecture out of the royal court; use timber and brick.

name: Ali Mech Guides Bakhtiyar Khalji's Horsemen
summary: At Devkot in March 1206, the Turkic general Bakhtiyar Khalji sets out toward Tibet with about 10,000 horsemen, led by the recently converted Mech tribal chief Ali Mech. He had invited the Rai of Kamrud to join; the Rai refused.
notes: Ali Mech has no person row yet (suggested id ali-mech). Route and numbers from Minhaj as relayed by later historians. Artistic reconstruction; early-13th-century raiders: mounted Turkic and Afghan troops in mail and quilted coats; foothill forest, Teesta valley.

name: The Broken Bridge on the Teesta
summary: On the retreat from Tibet the starving army, which has eaten its horses, finds the arches of the old stone bridge over the river broken and the supply line cut; the deep river kills men and horses at Devkot. Only about a hundred of the 10,000 return.
notes: Kamrup's role (cutting the bridge and supplies) rests on Bhattacharya's account; the king 'Prithu' is a later identification (low) and the 'Kanai-Barasi-Bowa' inscription is unverified. Bakhtiyar's death is disputed (illness or assassination by Ali Mardan). Artistic reconstruction; the broken bridge and river are the subject; show no clear Kamrup army.

name: Iwaz Khalji Is Turned Back Near Nagaon
summary: Bengal's Sultan Ghiyasuddin Iwaz Khalji campaigns up the valley as far as the Nagaon region, where the Gachtal inscription records his defeat. Coins suggest he may have reached Guwahati before returning to Lakhnauti, where Nasiruddin Mahmud captures and kills him.
notes: The reach of his campaign is disputed (Nagaon vs Guwahati). Artistic reconstruction; river fog and flooded fields; a small mounted force.

name: Nasiruddin Mahmud Crosses into Kamrup
summary: The Delhi prince Nasiruddin Mahmud, governor of Bengal, crosses through Jalpaiguri into Kamrup. The local king fortifies against him but is killed (an assassination plot is reported). A successor, Sandhya, is installed on condition of paying tribute.
notes: King's name 'Prithu' comes from later tradition (low). Sandhya's installation is the Wikipedia/Sarkar reconstruction (medium). Artistic reconstruction; show defences and the invaders' crossing; avoid portraying a named king.

name: Sandhya Stops the Tribute
summary: After Nasiruddin dies in 1229 and Bengal falls into confusion, Sandhya stops paying tribute, pushes the Muslim garrisons out, and extends his control to the Karatoya. He takes the title Gaudesvara after raiding across it.
notes: Details (Gaur raid, the title) rest on Sarkar and Acharyya via summaries; reconstructed. Artistic reconstruction; a royal court receives news; riverside garrison being withdrawn.

name: Yuzbak Occupies an Empty Kamarupanagara
summary: Malik Ikhtiyaruddin Yuzbak crosses the Karatoya near Goraghat, marches through Goalpara and enters the Kamarupa capital, which Sandhya has evacuated. There is little resistance ahead of him and effective resistance behind him. Yuzbak is said to have built the first mosque in Assam and had the khutbah read.
notes: Route per Sarkar. The mosque and khutbah claim is in the Wikipedia summary only. Artistic reconstruction; an empty but rich capital, invaders' camp, hills in the distance.

name: Sandhya Floods the Plain
summary: Sandhya retreats to the hills and, by tradition, dams a hill stream; when the spring rains come he releases the water and floods the plain, then cuts the invaders' supply line. A guide offers a shorter route through the foothills; the army is trapped in a narrow valley and destroyed. Yuzbak is captured (executed, July 1257) or dies of wounds.
notes: Strongest scene for 'geography beats armies'. The dam is Tradition; the flood and the supply cut are consistent across summaries. Yuzbak's death is disputed. Artistic reconstruction; flooded paddy, boats, soldiers on small high ground.

name: Sandhya Becomes Kamateswara at Kamatapur
summary: Sandhya moves his capital west from North Guwahati to Kamatapur, a more defensible site across rivers, and styles himself Kamateswara. Kamarupa becomes Kamata.
notes: Reconstructed; sources place Kamatapur near Cooch Behar or at Gosanimari. Artistic reconstruction; earth-and-brick rampart rising, river moat, new capital under construction; no stone citadel.

name: The Kacharis Turn Back Bahadur Shah
summary: Ghiyasuddin Bahadur Shah of Sonargaon moves up the old Brahmaputra and raids as far as Nagaon. Pratapdhwaj of Kamata's resistance is ineffective, but Kachari forces repel the sultan with heavy losses.
notes: Low confidence; single-source summary. Bahadur Shah was killed by Muhammad Tughlaq in 1327–28. Artistic reconstruction; river boats and Kachari warriors at a ford.

name: Durlabhnarayan and Dharmanarayan Divide the Kingdom
summary: After a succession dispute between cousins, a settlement splits Kamata: Durlabhnarayan keeps the western core including Kamatapur and Dharmanarayan keeps Rangpur and Mymensingh.
notes: Reconstructed; exact dates unknown. Rulers' dates in the CSV are 'reconstructed'. Artistic reconstruction; a council of ministers and Brahmin witnesses.

name: Chandivara's Fourteen Families Settle at Langamaguri
summary: Under the treaty between the two kings, Chandivara's group of seven Kayastha and seven Brahmin families (traditionally refugees from Kannauj) is settled at Langamaguri near Guwahati; later they move to Bordowa with royal support. Sankardev descends from this line.
notes: On Neog's reading; Amalendu Guha instead derives the Bhuyans from local landed intermediaries. Present as one view. Artistic reconstruction; families arriving by boat, with household goods, scribes and priests; Bhuyan costume direction from research/ahom/agent-guidance.md.

name: Hema Saraswati Recites the Prahlada Charita
summary: At the court of Durlabhnarayan, the poet Hema Saraswati recites the Prahlada Charita, regarded as the earliest known poem in Assamese; Harihara Vipra is another court poet.
notes: Dating of the poets is uncertain. Artistic reconstruction; palm-leaf or sanchi-pat manuscript, a lamp-lit hall, listening courtiers.

name: Madhav Kandali Writes the Saptakanda Ramayana
summary: At the command of Mahamanikya, a Barāha/Borahi king of the Nagaon–Morigaon–Hojai region, the poet Madhav Kandali translates the Sanskrit Ramayana into Assamese verse; the Lankākānda states this patronage.
notes: The poet's own statement in the Lankākānda is the evidence for Mahamanikya (medium). Mahamanikya's dynastic label varies (Barāha vs Borahi-Kachari). Artistic reconstruction; a poet at work with a manuscript; avoid temple architecture.

name: Ilyas Shah Takes Guwahati
summary: Shamsuddin Ilyas Shah of Bengal comes up the Brahmaputra through northern Mymensingh, enters Kamata's core and takes Guwahati. A coin dated 1357–59 minted at 'Chawlistan urf Kamrup' suggests occupation. He dies about November 1357.
notes: Coin evidence (medium). Kamata was weakened by Ahom and Kachari pressure and a breakaway chieftain (1329). Artistic reconstruction; river fleet, fort at Guwahati, hills on the horizon.

name: Sikandar Shah Met at Gachtal
summary: Sikandar Shah advances to the Kopili river, where Mahamanikya, Indranarayan of Kamata and the Bhuyan chiefs fight him at Gachtal near Nagaon.
notes: The outcome is not stated in the sources found; do not paint a decisive victory. Date flagged 'citation needed'. Artistic reconstruction; allied levies on the river bank, no winner shown.

name: Arimatta Seizes the Throne
summary: The Bhuyan Arimatta overthrows the weakened Indranarayan; his successors Gajanka, Sukranka and Mriganka hold Kamata until about 1440.
notes: Reconstructed; the Bhuyan interregnum has no firm narrative. Artistic reconstruction; a palace hall, armed Bhuyan retainers.

name: Kanta Nath Rises as Niladhwaj, First of the Khen Kings
summary: A man of humble origin, Kanta Nath, rises to found the Khen dynasty as Niladhwaj, and rules from Kamatapur.
notes: Origin stories conflict: a poor boy from Taluk Jambari (Gosani Mangala) vs a Tripura migrant. Ethnicity uncertain. Artistic reconstruction; coronation of a local chief; keep costume modest.

name: A Bhuyan Boyhood at Alipukhuri
summary: The orphaned boy Sankara (later Sankardev), raised by his grandmother Khersuti in a chief Baro-Bhuyan family near Bordowa, starts school under Mahendra Kandali at about age 12.
notes: Birthplace (Alipukhuri or Patekibari) and birth year (1449 or 1479–84) are disputed. Artistic reconstruction; a village house with a courtyard and a guru's tol.

name: Nilambar's Kamatapur
summary: The Khen king Nilambar rules from the great fortified capital at Kamatapur (Gosanimari): earth-and-brick ramparts, gates, moats and royal compounds.
notes: Gosanimari is the usual identification. Claims of wide conquest are uncited. Artistic reconstruction; an establishing view of the fortified capital; no stone or temple architecture.

name: Muzaffar Shah's Coins: Kamata Mardan
summary: Bengal's Sultan Shamsuddin Muzaffar Shah takes parts of Kamata and mints coins carrying the title 'Kamata Mardan' (conqueror of Kamata).
notes: Coin evidence (medium). Artistic reconstruction; a mint scene with a die-stamp and coins; or the sultan's officers in a captured town.

name: Sachipatra's Grievance
summary: The Brahmin minister Sachipatra, whose son was executed by Nilambar for an affair with the queen, goes to Husain Shah's court and urges him to invade.
notes: Tradition (low): a story that explains the invasion, not firm evidence. Mark clearly as legend in the viewer. Artistic reconstruction; a Brahmin petitioner at a Gaur court.

name: The Siege of Kamatapur
summary: Shah Ismail Ghazi, sent by Alauddin Husain Shah, besieges the fort of Kamatapur and destroys the city. Nilambar is imprisoned and the Khen dynasty ends.
notes: Dates conflict (siege from c. 1493; fall 1498; expedition 1499). Army sizes are uncited. Artistic reconstruction; river-borne army, earth ramparts, defenders on the walls.

name: Danyal Governs from Hajo
summary: Husain Shah's conquest reaches Hajo by 1502; his son Shahzada Danyal governs the conquered region. Husain Shah's coins call him 'conqueror of Kamru, Kamata, Jajnagar and Urisa' and a stone at Malda records the victory.
notes: Completion date from Sarkar (via summary). Artistic reconstruction; an administrative court with Bengali officials; Hajo's riverside.

name: The Bhuyans Destroy Danyal's Garrison
summary: Led by Harup Narayan of Bausi, the Baro-Bhuyans fall on Danyal's garrison and destroy it 'to the last man' (Baruah), ending Sultanate rule within about ten years of the conquest.
notes: Date is 1505 in one summary and later in others; Danyal's fate is described differently. Artistic reconstruction; night attack by Bhuyan irregulars; bamboo and earth defences.

name: Bisu Defeats the Bhuyan of Karnapur
summary: Bisu, son of the Mech chief Hariya Mandal and the Koch chief Hajo's daughter Hira, defeats the Bhuyan chiefs one by one; against the Bhuyan of Karnapur he needs a stratagem.
notes: The stratagem is not described in the sources read. He may first have fought under the Bhuyans against the Sultan. Artistic reconstruction; Koch and Mech warriors, forest-edge fortification.

name: Bisu Is Crowned Biswa Singha
summary: Bisu is crowned king of Kamata between the Karatoya and Barnadi rivers, takes the Hindu name Biswa Singha, and appoints his brother Sisu as yuvaraj. Later Brahmin pandits give him a divine descent from Shiva.
notes: Date 1515 is well attested; the Shiva legend is Legend (a later claim to Kshatriya status). Artistic reconstruction; a coronation with Brahmin priests; mix of tribal and Hindu elements.
